t: Encrypt and Decrypt Strings — Count Encryptions, Not Decryptions
o: Encryption maps each character to a fixed 2-letter code and is therefore deterministic; decryption is ambiguous because several keys may share one value (in Example 1 both 'a' and 'c' encode to "ei"). decrypt(word2) must return how many dictionary strings could have produced word2, which for "eizfeiam" is 2 ("abad" and "abcd"). Enumerating all possible originals explodes exponentially when many characters share codes, so instead we push every dictionary word through the deterministic encrypt() function and compare with word2: a word can decrypt to word2 if and only if encrypt(word) == word2. With at most 100 dictionary words of length up to 100 and only 200 calls total, this direction of reasoning is cheap; caching encrypted forms makes each query O(1).
k: Never enumerate decryptions — with shared values the candidate set grows exponentially; exploit that encryption is a well-defined function.
word could decrypt to word2 exactly when encrypt(word) equals word2, so count dictionary words whose encryption matches.
Precomputing encrypt(w) for all dictionary words in the constructor turns every decrypt call into one hash-map lookup.

a.n: Approach 1: Encrypt Dictionary on Every decrypt Call
a.i: Keep the dictionary as given. To answer decrypt(word2), run encrypt over each stored word and count exact string matches against word2. Encryption is linear in word length thanks to the key-to-value map, and with <= 100 words this stays comfortably within limits without any preprocessing bookkeeping.
s: Store key-to-value pairs in a hash map and keep the dictionary list.
encrypt(word1): append values[i] for each character via the map; return "" if any character is missing from keys.
decrypt(word2): for each dictionary word, compute its encryption.
Count words whose encryption equals word2 and return the count.
a.t: encrypt O(L); decrypt O(D * L) where D = 100 dictionary words of length L <= 100.
a.sp: O(D * L + K) — dictionary storage plus the key map.

a.i: All decryption answers depend only on which encrypted strings occur in the dictionary, so build a frequency map from encrypted string to word count during construction. Each decrypt(word2) then returns cnt[word2] instantly, and encrypt remains an O(L) map walk. This front-loads work once instead of repeating it on up to 200 calls.
s: For every dictionary word, compute encrypt(word) and increment its count in a hash map.
a.t: constructor O(D * L); encrypt O(L); decrypt O(1) expected hash lookup.
a.sp: O(D * L + K) — encrypted-form counts plus the key map.

w: The crucial interview point is refusing to brute-force decryptions: state the iff condition encrypt(w) == word2, then pick Approach 2 for optimal query time (mention Approach 1 as the straightforward version). Pitfalls: treating decrypt as producing one canonical original rather than counting candidates, forgetting the empty-string return when a character is absent from keys, and double-counting identical dictionary entries — the counter handles multiplicity correctly. Edge cases include word2 that no dictionary word encrypts to (answer 0). Follow-ups: support streaming dictionary updates (rebuild or use incremental counters), or answer decrypt without storing plaintexts.
